title: Dreams
objective: After this level you can describe what scientists know about why we dream.
summary: In the early 1950s, rapid eye movements in sleep were found and linked to dreaming. Why we dream is still open: wishes, random signals and memory are rival theories.

cards.headline: In 1951, a machine said a sleeping boy was wide awake.
cards.body: Eugene Aserinsky taped electrodes to his 8-year-old son Armond's head and put him to bed. Hours later, the pens were swinging as if the boy were alert and looking around. Aserinsky went in to check. Armond's eyes were closed. He was fast asleep.

cards.fact: Wake someone when their eyes dart, and they'll tell you a dream.
cards.context: In 1953, Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago reported regular periods of rapid eye movements in sleep. Sleepers woken during them had been dreaming, often vividly. Today we know everyone dreams, for about two hours a night, and dreams happen in all stages but are usually most vivid in REM sleep. Most are forgotten by breakfast.

items.label: Activation-synthesis
points: The brainstem fires signals in REM
The forebrain builds a story from them

cards.headline: No winner yet
cards.body: Here's the honest part: the exact purpose of dreaming is not known. Each theory explains some things about dreams, and none has settled the question. So treat any confident claim about what dreams are for as a theory, not a verdict.

mascot.line: If anyone tells you exactly what last night's dream meant, they know more than the scientists do.

questions.prompt: In which kind of sleep are dreams usually most vivid?

options.label: Stage 1, the changeover
options.rationale: Dreams can happen there, but REM dreams are most vivid.

options.label: Stage 3, deep sleep
options.rationale: Dreams can occur in all stages, but not most vividly here.

questions.explanation: Dreams can happen in all sleep stages, but they are usually most vivid in REM sleep.

questions.prompt: According to the activation-synthesis hypothesis, where do dreams come from?

options.label: The forebrain making a story from signals fired in REM

questions.explanation: Hobson and McCarley proposed that the brainstem fires signals during REM and the forebrain builds a story to make sense of them.
